title: Synergistic Role of Lignocellulosic Nanomaterials and Microbial Consortia in Wastewater Treatment
content:
Lignocellulosic nanomaterials integrated with microbial consortia provide a sustainable platform for enhanced pollutant adsorption, biofilm-mediated degradation, and redox-driven remediation. This synergistic approach improves removal of heavy metals, pharmaceuticals, and industrial contaminants while supporting scalable and eco-friendly wastewater treatment technologies.


ABSTRACT

The integration of lignocellulosic nanomaterials (LCNMs) with microbial consortia offers an eco-sustainable strategy to address challenges in wastewater treatment and environmental remediation. LCNMs, derived from agricultural residues, possess high surface area, tunable chemistry, and strong pollutant-binding capacity, whereas microbial consortia provide diverse enzymatic systems for the degradation of contaminants, including heavy metals, pharmaceutical residues, dyes, and industrial waste. This review examines the synergistic interactions between LCNMs and microorganisms, emphasizing enhanced pollutant adsorption, redox mediation, biofilm formation, and enzyme immobilization as key mechanisms that drive improved contaminant removal. Applications in heavy metal sequestration, pharmaceutical degradation, and constructed wetland systems are discussed, together with challenges related to material stability, scalability, and ecotoxicological safety. Future perspectives include AI-guided process optimization, genetic engineering of microbial communities, and circular economy approaches utilizing lignocellulosic waste for nanomaterial production. Advances in LCNM–microbial technologies represent scalable, adaptable, and green solutions for next-generation wastewater treatment systems. Overall, LCNM–microbial technologies have demonstrated considerable potential for the removal of diverse pollutants under laboratory and pilot-scale conditions. However, challenges related to material durability, ecotoxicological safety, process standardization, and regulatory acceptance continue to limit their large-scale implementation, highlighting the need for further multidisciplinary research.
